analysis.one_liner: Doubles and triples damages for unpaid wages, requires paystubs, and bans forced arbitration of wage claims.
analysis.headline: The Wage Theft Prevention and Wage Recovery Act, introduced with 37 House cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets wage theft — employers not paying minimum wage, skipping overtime, requiring off-the-clock work, or withholding final paychecks. It would require employers to give workers detailed paystubs and disclose pay rates at hire, pay workers the rate in their contract even when it exceeds the minimum wage, and pay final wages within 14 days of a job ending. It doubles the damages owed for unpaid wages, triples them for workers who are fired or punished for complaining, extends the time limit for suing from 2 years to 4, bans employment contracts that force workers to give up their right to sue over wages, and funds $50 million a year in grants to help community groups detect violations and recover back pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers, who bear the brunt of wage theft — the bill cites studies estimating workers lose more than $8.6 billion a year, with women, immigrants, and Black workers hit hardest. Workers would get paystubs that show exactly how their pay was calculated, higher damages when they win a case, four to five years instead of two or three to file a claim, and the right to sue even if they signed an arbitration agreement. Honest employers who already follow the law would no longer compete against companies that cut costs by not paying earned wages.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to give every worker a paystub showing hours worked, pay rate, overtime, and each deduction, and to disclose pay rate and employment classification within 15 days of hiring. [S2] [S3]

Doubles the damages an employer must pay for unpaid wages (from one extra amount to two times the unpaid wages, plus interest), and triples them for workers who are retaliated against for whistleblowing. [S2] [S3]

Bans employers from requiring workers to waive their right to sue over wages, including in pre-dispute arbitration agreements, and removes the requirement that workers opt in in writing to join a collective lawsuit. [S2] [S3]
Extends the statute of limitations for wage claims from 2 years to 4 (5 for willful or repeat violations), and pauses the clock while the Labor Department investigates. [S2] [S3]

Requires employers to pay a fired or departing worker all unpaid hours within 14 days, with daily wages owed beyond that, and gives workers the right to inspect up to five years of their own pay records, with a presumption favoring the worker's evidence if the employer's records are incomplete. [S2] [S3]
Authorizes $50 million per year through fiscal 2020 for grants to community organizations and other eligible entities to educate workers, detect violations, and help recover back pay. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers that fail to pay earned wages — they would owe double or triple damages plus interest, higher fines, and possible Justice Department referral for willful offenders. All covered employers would also bear the cost of producing detailed paystubs and hire-date disclosures, though many states already require similar paystubs.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on all covered employers, including small businesses, which must produce detailed paystubs, hire-date disclosures, and five years of back pay records on request. [S3]

Doubling and tripling damages and eliminating written consent for joining collective suits raises litigation exposure for employers, and critics would argue this invites more lawsuits rather than more compliance; the bill's findings counter that current penalties are too weak to deter repeat violators. [S2] [S3]

The ban on pre-dispute arbitration waivers overrides the Federal Arbitration Act for wage claims, which supporters view as restoring workers' day in court and opponents view as stripping a dispute-resolution choice employers and workers contract for. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: workers keep what they earn, and employers that underpay face real penalties. The record the bill itself compiles — $8.6 billion a year in stolen wages, repeat offenders continuing to violate, and workers in some states with no protection at all — supports stronger remedies. The main honest costs are paperwork for compliant employers and increased litigation risk from multiplied damages, which fall heaviest on small businesses that are also frequent victims of low-road competitors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and later sent to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended — no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on March 16, 2016, joined by 30 original cosponsors. [S3]
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [S5]
On September 19, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections — its last action. [S5]
The bill's full action history ends there; the Republican-majority committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and no vote ever took place in either chamber. [S5] [S1]
All 37 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who underpay workers came out ahead: with no penalties raised, no paystub mandate, and no arbitration ban, the incentives the bill's findings describe — weak damages, repeat violations, and retaliation against complaining workers — remained unchanged. Workers owed unpaid wages kept the same narrow remedies.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 30 original cosponsors.

for.name: 37 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 37 were Democrats and none was a Republican.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction but never scheduled a hearing or markup; it was sent to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections in September 2016 and stayed there until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Brought no wage-theft bill to the floor during the 114th Congress; the bill never advanced beyond subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican sponsored the bill, in a House where Republicans held the majority and controlled the committee calendar.

industries.industry: Employers in low-wage, high-violation industries (fast food, restaurants, retail, janitorial, construction)
industries.note: The bill's findings cite compliance below 50 percent in some industries and $8.6 billion a year in unpaid wages; doubled damages, longer filing windows, and a ban on arbitration waivers directly raise the cost of underpaying workers. These are the interests that benefited most from the bill going nowhere.

The bill's findings state that noncompliant employers put compliant ones at a competitive disadvantage; tougher penalties for violators would level the field for businesses that already pay correctly, at the cost of new paystub and disclosure paperwork.
